title: Homework Week 8
intro: 6 questions + 1 optional challenge. Do each one on paper first (show your steps!), then check your answer here. Stuck? Use the hint ladder — but you earn more stars the fewer hints you need.

questions.text: Alex pays $2.25 to take the bus. Sam pays $3.00 to take the bus. If they each take the bus 20 times, how much less would Alex pay than Sam in total?
hints: Two ways: find each person’s total, or find how much less Alex pays for ONE ride.
The question asks for the **difference** between the two totals.

traps.3: $45 is what Alex pays in total — but the question asks how much LESS he pays than Sam.
traps.4: $60 is Sam’s total. You need the difference between the two totals.

solution: Shortcut: one ride is $0.75 less, so 20 rides is 20 × 0.75 = $15.
questions.idea: Rate: find the amount for ONE, then scale.

questions.text: The mean (average) of the numbers 20, 30, 40 is equal to the mean of the numbers
hints: Find the mean of 20, 30, 40 first.
The mean is 30, and there are 3 numbers — so the total must be 3 × 30 = 90.
Add up each option. Which one makes exactly 90?
solution: Mean of 20, 30, 40 = 90 ÷ 3 = 30, so the new numbers must also total 90.
questions.idea: Same mean and same count ⇒ same total.

questions.text: A jacket has a price tag of $80. It is on sale for 25% off. At the till, 15% tax is then added to the sale price. How much does Mia pay?
hints: Write each change as a multiplier. 25% off → × 0.75. Tax 15% → × 1.15.
80 × 0.75 = 60 (the sale price). Then the tax goes on the **sale price**.

traps.0: $60 is the sale price — you forgot the tax at the till.
traps.2: $72 comes from −25% + 15% = −10% off. But percent changes MULTIPLY, they don’t add: 0.75 × 1.15 ≈ 0.8625.
traps.4: $92 is $80 + 15% tax with no sale. The sale comes first!

questions.idea: Percent change = multiply by a factor.

questions.text: Joe filled up his car’s gas tank. After travelling 165 km, [[3/8]] of the gas in the tank was used. At this rate, approximately how much farther can the car travel before its fuel tank is completely empty?
hints: Find the km for ONE eighth of the tank: 165 km covers three eighths.
165 ÷ 3 = 55 km per eighth of a tank.
How many eighths of the tank are still left? Careful — the question asks how much *farther*.

traps.1: 440 km is the distance for the WHOLE tank. He has already driven 165 km of that.

solution: ONE eighth of the tank: 165 ÷ 3 = 55 km.
Left in the tank: 8 − 3 = 5 eighths → 5 × 55 = **275 km** → **(E)**.
questions.idea: Find the distance for ONE part, then scale.

questions.text: A bike is priced at $200. The store takes 20% off. Club members then take another 25% off the sale price. Finally, 15% tax is added. What is the final price?
hints: Three changes, three multipliers: × 0.80, × 0.75, × 1.15.
The second 25% comes off the **sale price**, not off the original $200.
200 × 0.80 × 0.75 × 1.15 — do it one step at a time.

traps.0: $110 is 55% of $200. That comes from adding 20% + 25% = 45% off. Successive changes multiply instead: 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.6, which is 40% off. (And you forgot the tax!)
traps.1: $126.50 = $110 × 1.15 — it adds 20% + 25% = 45% off first. Percent changes multiply, they don’t add.
traps.4: $160 is only the first discount (20% off). There are two more steps.

questions.idea: Successive changes MULTIPLY — they don’t add.

questions.text: Five friends buy tickets to a show. Early-bird tickets are 15% off the original price. The group also gets “buy 4, get 1 free”, so the 5 friends pay for only 4 tickets. Then 15% tax is added to the total, and the friends split the final bill equally. Each friend pays $58.65. What was the original price of one ticket?
hints: Undo the story in reverse order. To undo a multiplier, **divide** by it.
5 friends × $58.65 = the final bill. That bill had 15% tax added (× 1.15).
Divide by 1.15 to remove the tax, then ÷ 4 (only 4 tickets paid for), then ÷ 0.85 to undo the early-bird discount.
solution: Only 4 tickets were paid for: 255 ÷ 4 = $63.75 per early-bird ticket.
questions.idea: Working backward: undo each multiplier by dividing — in reverse order.

questions.text:
The heights of 4 athletes on a team are 135 cm, 160 cm, 170 cm, and 175 cm. Laurissa joins the team. On the new team of 5 athletes, the mode height of the players is equal to the median height which is equal to the mean (average) height. How tall is Laurissa?
Hint: Mode = the value that appears most often. Median = the middle value once the numbers are in order.
Example: 2, 2, 3, 4, 5 → mode = 2, median = 3.
hints: For there to be a mode, one height has to appear twice — so Laurissa must match one of the four existing heights (or 148 would leave no mode at all).
Try each candidate: put the 5 heights in order, find the middle one (median), and find the total ÷ 5 (mean).
If Laurissa is 170: median 170, but the mean is 810 ÷ 5 = 162. Not equal. Try 160.

traps.2: If Laurissa is 170, mode and median are both 170 — but the mean is 810 ÷ 5 = 162. All three must match.

solution: Mode needs a repeated value, so Laurissa copies one of 135, 160, 170, 175.
Laurissa = 170: median 170 but mean 162 ✗. Laurissa = 175: median 170 ✗. Laurissa = 135: mode 135 but median 160 ✗.
questions.idea: When three conditions must agree, test the candidates one at a time.
